newsitem.title: PERU: Press wreck homes to gain best view at Peru siege.
newsitem.headline: Press wreck homes to gain best view at Peru siege.

text.p: Hundreds of journalists swarming around the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima have wreaked havoc on neighbouring homes in their bid to secure the best view of the 5-day-old siege, witnesses said.

"We broke drainage piping and electricity cables," said Manuel Llanos, one of several photographers who clambered up to the roof of a neighbouring house that afforded a bird's eye view of the unfolding drama inside the compound.
The home's owners had given water to the 17 reporters on their roof and allowed them to use the bathroom.
While some journalists tried to make amends and collected money to pay for repairs, neighbours fed up with the media's behaviour struck back.
Peru's Channel 13 complained that one house owner had deliberately cut through its television transmission cables and prevented them from transmitting images from one roof.
"We are trying to cooperate with the media, but there's so much noise we cannot sleep," said resident Lula Melgar. "Suddenly this calm neighbourhood is nothing but one huge din."
Some residents charged for access to their roofs, some in the form of tolls. Others rented out their space for up to $1,000.
"There are a lot of press people paying for roofs. I paid 100 soles ($40) for three nights," said Llanos, tanned after his constant vigil in the Lima sun.

Nine journalists spent the first three nights of the siege stuck on a nearby roof, unwilling to give up their grandstand view after police told them they would not be able to return to the now sealed-off site.

Then, after the police granted free access to the prized roof, the disgruntled houseowner left about a dozen of the press stranded when she locked up her house and declared she was going to spend Christmas with her sister, a Reuter photographer at the scene said.
